title: Solve sampling problems with or without replacement
show: probability tree for three draws without replacement from 7 red and 5 blue, with changing denominators

example.question: A bag holds 7 red counters and 5 blue counters. Three counters are drawn at random, one after another, without replacement. Find the probability that exactly two of them are red.

steps.say: Exactly two red means one blue. The blue can come first, second or third, so there are three orders: $RRB$, $RBR$ and $BRR$. Each order has the same probability, so find one and multiply.
Without replacement the bag shrinks. After each draw, the number of counters left drops by one. Multiply the three fractions for $RRB$.
The three orders are separate outcomes, so add them. That is the same as multiplying one order by $\hl{2}{3}$.

title: Continue and generalise a pattern
show: the first three tile patterns with 6, 10, 14 tiles drawn, each growing by 4

example.question:
The first three patterns in a sequence use 6, 10 and 14 tiles. The pattern continues in the same way.
(a) Find the number of tiles in patterns 4 and 5.
(b) Write the number of tiles in pattern $n$ in terms of $n$.
(c) Which pattern uses 102 tiles?

steps.say: Look at how much each pattern adds. If it is the same every time, the pattern is arithmetic.

rows.aside: $14-10 = 4$ as well, so the difference is always 4.

steps.say: Add $\hl{1}{4}$ each time.
Use $T_n = a + (n-1)d$ with $a = 6$ and $d = \hl{1}{4}$.
Set $T_n$ equal to 102 and solve for $n$.

title: Draw bar, pie, line plot, histogram and stem-and-leaf
show: pie chart with angles for Bus 144°, Car 108°, Walk 72°, Cycle 36° and a matching bar chart

example.question:
60 students were asked how they travel to school.
Bus: 24, Car: 18, Walk: 12, Cycle: 6
Find the angle for each sector of a pie chart of this data.

steps.say: A pie chart is a full circle, $360^\circ$, shared among all $60$ students. Divide to find the angle for one student.
Multiply each frequency by $\hl{1}{6}$.
The sectors must fill the circle. Add the angles and check you get $360^\circ$.

rows.aside: Now draw each sector with a protractor and label it with its group name.

title: Find quartiles and the interquartile range
show: box plot of 4,7,8,11,13,15,18,20 with Q1, median, Q3 marked and IQR bracket

example.question:
The number of text messages Aoife sent on eight days was:
$11, 4, 18, 7, 20, 13, 8, 15$
Find the interquartile range.

steps.say: Write the numbers in order, smallest first. With eight numbers the median sits between the 4th and 5th, so it splits the list into two halves of four.
$\hl{1}{Q_1}$ is the median of the lower half. Four numbers, so take the middle two and find their mean.
$\hl{2}{Q_3}$ is the median of the upper half. Same method on $13, 15, 18, 20$.
The interquartile range is $\hl{2}{Q_3}$ minus $\hl{1}{Q_1}$.

title: Read scatter plots and correlation
show: scatter plot of the five (x,y) points showing the trend direction

example.question:
A teacher records hours of TV watched, $x$, and test score, $y$, for five students.
$x$: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5
$y$: 9, 7, 6, 3, 2
The points lie close to a straight line sloping downhill. Choose the value of $r$ from $0.99$, $-0.2$, $-0.99$ and explain your choice.

steps.say: Look at which way the points run. As $x$ goes up, $y$ goes down, so the **direction** is negative. That rules out $0.99$.
Look at how tight the points are. They lie close to one straight line, so the link is **strong**. A value near $0$, like $-0.2$, means a loose cloud.

rows.aside: Close to a line: strong, so $r$ is near $-1$

steps.say: Strong and negative means $r$ is close to $-1$. Give the value, then say it in words.

rows.aside: Strong negative linear correlation: as TV time goes up, test score goes down.

title: Recognise outliers
show: box plot with fences at Q1-1.5IQR and Q3+1.5IQR and the outlier point marked beyond

example.question:
Find any outliers in this data set, using the rule that an outlier lies more than $1.5 \times \text{IQR}$ above $Q_3$ or below $Q_1$.
$3, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 11, 30$

steps.say: The data is already in order. Find $\hl{1}{Q_1}$ and $\hl{2}{Q_3}$, the medians of the lower and upper halves.
Subtract the quartiles to get the width of the middle half.
Go $1.5 \times \text{IQR}$ beyond each quartile. Beyond these, a value is an outlier.
Check the smallest and largest values against the fences. Only $30$ is outside.
